title: Stone Line
subtitle: Three ages of the wall that guarded an empire

chapters.label: CHAPTER 01 · EARLY FORTIFICATIONS
chapters.heading: Stone and earth stitched across warring states.
chapters.subheading: Walls rose long before a single emperor.
chapters.body: The first walls date to the 7th century BC. During the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods the states of Zheng, Chu, Qin, Wei, Zhao, Qi, Lu, Han, Yan, Zhongshan and Zhou built extensive stone or rammed-earth ramparts. After Qin unified the realm in 221 BC the new ruler ordered the old sections destroyed and began linking the remaining fortifications along the northern frontier.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 02 · MING REINFORCEMENT
chapters.heading: Bricks rose where earth once lay.
chapters.subheading: The Ming forged a stronger barrier.
chapters.body: Following defeat at the Battle of Tumu the Ming dynasty built new walls using bricks and stone instead of rammed earth. Up to 25,000 watchtowers were erected. Between 1567 and 1570 General Qi Jiguang supervised the construction of 1,200 towers from Shanhaiguan Pass to Changping, and many plain earth sections were faced with brick, especially near Beijing.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 03 · MANCHU INVADE
chapters.heading: The gates opened on May 25, ending a dynasty.
chapters.subheading: A decisive breach at Shanhai Pass.
chapters.body: In 1644 the Ming general Wu Sangui opened the gates of Shanhai Pass on May 25, allying with the Manchus. The Manchus crossed the Great Wall, seized Beijing and ended the Ming dynasty. Earlier raids had crossed the wall, but this was the first full conquest through the fortified pass.
